screens.title: Functions, Modules, and Libraries
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on three tightly related habits that make Raspberry Pi projects manageable: writing functions, organizing code into modules, and using libraries. You will learn to encapsulate behavior with functions, pass inputs and receive outputs, and decide when a small helper belongs in a shared module. We also cover Python's built-in modules you use often, how to add third-party packages with the package installer, and why virtual environments protect your project. Practically, this matters because Raspberry Pi projects blend hardware, data logging, networking, and interfaces. Clear functions and modular files reduce bugs and speed debugging when a sensor or camera misbehaves. For example, a conversions module holds temperature and length conversions so every script uses the same tested routines. Later, we show how to create and activate a virtual environment and install gpiozero so your GPIO code runs safely without altering system packages. As you move through the chapter, think of modules like kitchen stations and functions like recipes — that analogy will guide practical organization and testing.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to write clear functions with parameters and return values, organize code into reusable modules, and use both Python's standard library and third-party libraries on a Raspberry Pi. You will also learn how to create and use a virtual environment and install packages with the package installer, keeping project dependencies isolated. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: functions reduce repetition and make testing easier; modules group related behavior so the project scales; libraries let you control hardware and run web services without rewriting common code. For example, after you define a conversion function once, every script can import it and rely on consistent behavior. You'll practice installing gpiozero inside a virtual environment and importing it into a small script to read a sensor. A common misconception is that installing globally is simpler — instead, using a virtual environment avoids version conflicts that later break other projects. These objectives prepare you to build dependable Raspberry Pi projects that are easy to extend.

screens.title: Objective Details & Learning Path
screens.narratorSegment: Let's unpack the objectives with practical outcomes. First, defining functions means you can take a repeated task, like converting sensor readings, and place it in one tested routine. A mastery check is that you can write a function that accepts parameters, uses default values when appropriate, and returns results reliably for other parts of the program to consume. Second, organizing modules means you separate hardware code, UI code, and web code into named files, and import only what you need. A practical test is building a small project with a sensors module and a display module that import cleanly. Third, using libraries requires familiarity with Python's standard helpers such as json and time and with third-party packages like gpiozero for GPIO control. You should be able to install a package and import it without affecting other projects. Finally, dependency management with virtual environments means you can create, activate, and deactivate an environment, then install packages into it. Misconception: virtual environments are optional — in practice they prevent hard-to-debug conflicts and make deployments repeatable.

screens.title: What is a function?
screens.narratorSegment: A function is a named block of code that performs a single, focused task and can be used repeatedly with different inputs. In Python you declare a function using the def keyword, give it a name, list parameters, and return a value. For example, a function that converts Celsius readings to Fahrenheit encapsulates the formula once so every script reuses the same logic. That reduces duplication and the chance of errors when the formula needs to change. The practical example you will see on the screen shows a conversion routine, an example call that converts twenty five degrees, and a print that outputs the result. A frequent misconception is that functions are only for large programs; in fact, even small scripts benefit because functions make intent explicit and simplify testing. When you write tests, you can call the function directly and check its return value. A closing tip: name functions with a clear verb phrase, keep them short, and make side effects explicit. Which small task in your project could become a function today? What is a function? means encapsulate a single task into a named routine with inputs and outputs for reuse and testability.. In practical terms, a reusable block that performs one task. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Chapter 3.4 › What is a function?
Definition & purpose

Functions reduce repetition, clarify intent, and allow unit testing of small pieces of logic. They accept parameters and return values.

Common mistakes
  • Making functions do too many things instead of one clear task.
  • Relying heavily on global state instead of passing needed values as parameters.
Key Takeaway

Choose clear names, keep functions focused, and return values for predictable composition.

Example: Celsius to Fahrenheit
def celsius_to_fahrenheit(celsius):
    return (celsius * 9/5) + 32

temp_f = celsius_to_fahrenheit(25)
print(temp_f)
This example shows declaration, a call with an input, and output. Tests can call the function with multiple inputs to verify correctness.
Analogy: a single recipe that produces consistent results when you supply different ingredients.

screens.title: Parameters, Defaults, and Multiple Returns
screens.narratorSegment: Parameters let functions accept different input values so the same routine handles many cases. Python supports positional parameters, keyword parameters, and default values that provide sensible fallbacks. The source example describes a sensor with a name, numeric value, and a unit that defaults to the string units when none is supplied. That default helps when a caller doesn't need to specify units every time. Functions may also return multiple values by packaging them into a tuple; consumers can unpack those values as needed. A practical tip is to prefer explicit return values and avoid silently returning None. A common misconception is that default parameters are good for mutable objects — in Python, using mutable defaults can lead to shared state across calls; prefer None and create a new object inside the function when needed. The example here is concrete: describe_sensor returns a formatted string for display, and default unit makes calls simpler. When you design functions for hardware projects, think about what must be passed, what can default, and how callers will use returned values. Parameters, Defaults, and Multiple Returns means use parameters and sensible defaults to make functions flexible, and return explicit values for predictable composition.. In practical terms, designing flexible function interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Parameters › Chapter 3.4 › Parameters & Returns
How parameters work
Parameters are placeholders for values the caller provides. Defaults supply fallback values so callers can omit arguments when the default is acceptable.
Misconception
Avoid using mutable default parameters; they can persist unexpected state across calls. Use None and create new objects inside the function instead.
Pro Tip

Design defaults that reflect common usage so most calls remain concise.

Concrete example
def describe_sensor(name, value, unit="units"):
    return f"{name}: {value} {unit}"

print(describe_sensor("Temperature", 22.5, "°C"))
print(describe_sensor("Humidity", 60, "%"))
This shows a default unit value and two calls: one that specifies a unit and one that relies on the default. Returning a formatted string lets other parts of the program display consistent sensor labels.

screens.title: From Functions to Modules
screens.narratorSegment: As projects grow, keeping every function in one script becomes unwieldy. A module is simply a Python file that groups related functions, classes, and constants. The process of deciding when to create a module is practical: when a set of functions serve a shared purpose — conversions, sensor reading, display formatting — move them into a module file with a descriptive name. The recipe-like kitchen analogy helps: imagine each module as a station that holds its recipes and tools: a conversions module is the spice rack, sensors module the produce station, and display module the plating station. When you import a module, you reuse tested routines and keep the main script focused on high-level orchestration. A common mistake is circular imports: avoid modules importing each other in a loop. Prefer clear top-level responsibilities and use small helper modules. This screen shows a three-step flow: identify related functions, create a module file, then import and call the routines from your main script. As a question, consider which functions in your project belong together as a module. From Functions to Modules means group functions by purpose into modules to improve clarity and reuse; treat modules like kitchen stations.. In practical terms, when to move code into a module. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow › Chapter 3.4 › From Functions to Modules
Three-step process
  1. Identify related functions that change together or share responsibility.
  2. Create a module file, e.g. conversions.py, sensors.py, display.py, and move functions there.
  3. Import specific functions into scripts to keep the main program concise.
Avoid circular imports by keeping modules' top-level behavior minimal and importing only the functions you need.
Key Takeaway

Modules group responsibilities. Import what you need and keep module interfaces small and stable.

Analogy: kitchen stations
Each module is an ingredient station with recipes. The main script orchestrates stations to produce the final dish.
Example layout
sensors.py — sensor read functions; display.py — rendering helpers; webapp.py — web endpoints. Import these modules into a central runner script.

screens.title: Standard Library vs Third-Party Libraries

Third-party libraries add domain-specific features, like gpiozero for GPIO control, picamera2 for camera access, flask for a web interface, and paho-mqtt for MQTT messaging. On Raspberry Pi projects, you typically combine standard library modules with third-party packages: use json to parse configuration files and gpiozero to read sensors. A misconception is that third-party libraries are unsafe; they are essential but should be vetted and installed into a project-specific environment. When deciding what to use, prefer standard modules for core tasks and add third-party packages only when they save substantial work. In practical terms, what comes with python and what you install. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Comparison › Chapter 3.4 › Standard vs Third-Party
Standard library
  • time, datetime — sleep, timestamps, and delays
  • json — read and write configuration and structured data
  • csv — read/write CSV files for logs
  • os, sys — file paths and process-level utilities
  • random, math, statistics — common computations
These modules require no installation and form the backbone of many Pi scripts.
Third-party libraries
Examples on Raspberry Pi include gpiozero, RPi.GPIO, smbus2, spidev, picamera2, flask, and paho-mqtt. These provide hardware and service integrations that simplify development.
Misconception
Not all third-party packages are heavy; some are thin wrappers that save a lot of boilerplate. Evaluate stability and community adoption before depending on them.

screens.title: Using json to Read Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Reading configuration from a file is an everyday task. Python's json module makes it simple to read structured data and access fields by key. The example on screen opens a config. json file, parses it into a Python dictionary, and prints a sensor interval value. This pattern decouples configuration from code so you can tune behavior without editing your scripts. A common mistake is assuming the file always exists or contains the expected keys; robust code checks for file existence and uses defaults if keys are missing. In hardware projects, configuration often contains pin numbers, polling intervals, and network settings; keeping them in JSON makes deployments repeatable. When testing, create a minimal config file with the keys your script expects, and add error handling for missing or malformed files. A practical testing step is to change the sensor interval in the JSON and rerun the script to observe the new polling behavior. What default would you choose if the config file is absent? Code Walkthrough › Chapter 3.4 › Read JSON config
Code example
import json

with open("config.json", "r") as f:
    config = json.load(f)

print(config["sensor_interval"])
This reads the file, parses it, and accesses a key. Add checks for missing files and missing keys before using values in production.
Best practices
  • Provide sensible defaults when keys are missing.
  • Validate types — ensure a polling interval is numeric and within expected bounds.
  • Keep sensitive secrets out of plain JSON in production.
Check

If the config file is missing, decide a safe default and log a warning rather than crashing.

screens.title: Create and Use a Virtual Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Virtual environments create isolated Python environments for each project so packages you install do not affect the system Python or other projects. The process is straightforward: create an environment, activate it, install packages, and deactivate when finished. The chapter's example uses the module invoked by python three to create a venv directory, then sources the activate script and installs gpiozero and flask. Activating the environment changes the shell's path so pip installs into the environment rather than the global site-packages. This isolation avoids the common problem where two projects need incompatible package versions. A practical test is to create the environment, install gpiozero, then run a small script that imports the module; when you deactivate and try to run the script without activation, the import should fail, demonstrating isolation. A common misconception is that virtual environments duplicate the system Python; they are lightweight links around that interpreter and only add isolated package directories. Use them for any project that has external dependencies. Create and Use a Virtual Environment means create isolated environments per project to install packages safely and avoid global conflicts.. In practical terms, isolate dependencies for each project. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process › Chapter 3.4 › Virtual Environment
Commands to run
python3 -m venv myproject_env
source myproject_env/bin/activate
pip install gpiozero flask
# when done
deactivate
These commands create, activate, install packages into, and deactivate a project environment.
Why it matters
Environments prevent version conflicts and make your project reproducible. When sharing code, include a requirements file listing package versions.
Misconception

Virtual environments are not heavyweight virtual machines; they are isolated package directories around the same interpreter.

Hands-on › Chapter 3.4 › Create conversions.py
conversions.py (example)
def celsius_to_fahrenheit(celsius):
    return (celsius * 9/5) + 32

def cm_to_inches(cm):
    return cm / 2.54

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(celsius_to_fahrenheit(0))

Importer script
from conversions import celsius_to_fahrenheit

readings = [22.5, 18.0, 25.0]
for r in readings:
    print(celsius_to_fahrenheit(r))

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Working with functions, modules, and environments has common pitfalls you can avoid with simple habits. First, putting hardware initialization code at import time causes tests and imports to fail; instead, provide an explicit initialize function the main script calls. Second, circular imports occur when modules import each other — break responsibilities or use local imports inside functions to avoid loops. Third, using mutable default arguments leads to shared state across function calls; use None and create fresh objects inside the function. Fourth, installing packages globally can create version conflicts; always prefer a virtual environment per project. Fifth, forgetting to include a module's path causes ImportError; keep modules in the project folder or install them into the virtual environment. For each mistake, the remedy is clear: explicit initialization, small module interfaces, safe default patterns, per-project environments, and reproducible requirements files. As a final check, run your code in a fresh virtual environment to confirm your requirements are complete. screens.narratorSegment: Keep three practical concepts top of mind. First, functions are small, focused recipes: name them clearly, pass necessary parameters, and return explicit results for composition and testing. Second, modules group related functions and classes into files that act like kitchen stations; import only what you need and avoid side effects on import. These ideas together let you scale a project from a script to a maintainable system that interacts with sensors, cameras, and networks without turning into a tangled codebase. When you start a new Pi project, sketch the module layout and list required libraries first — that planning step saves debugging time later.

In this chapter we focus on three tightly related habits that make Raspberry Pi projects manageable: writing functions, organizing code into modules, and using libraries. You will learn to encapsulate behavior with functions, pass inputs and receive outputs, and decide when a small helper belongs in a shared module. We also cover Python's built-in modules you use often, how to add third-party packages with the package installer, and why virtual environments protect your project. Practically, this matters because Raspberry Pi projects blend hardware, data logging, networking, and interfaces. Clear functions and modular files reduce bugs and speed debugging when a sensor or camera misbehaves. For example, a conversions module holds temperature and length conversions so every script uses the same tested routines. Later, we show how to create and activate a virtual environment and install gpiozero so your GPIO code runs safely without altering system packages. As you move through the chapter, think of modules like kitchen stations and functions like recipes — that analogy will guide practical organization and testing.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to write clear functions with parameters and return values, organize code into reusable modules, and use both Python's standard library and third-party libraries on a Raspberry Pi. You will also learn how to create and use a virtual environment and install packages with the package installer, keeping project dependencies isolated. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: functions reduce repetition and make testing easier; modules group related behavior so the project scales; libraries let you control hardware and run web services without rewriting common code. For example, after you define a conversion function once, every script can import it and rely on consistent behavior. You'll practice installing gpiozero inside a virtual environment and importing it into a small script to read a sensor. A common misconception is that installing globally is simpler — instead, using a virtual environment avoids version conflicts that later break other projects. These objectives prepare you to build dependable Raspberry Pi projects that are easy to extend.

Let's unpack the objectives with practical outcomes. First, defining functions means you can take a repeated task, like converting sensor readings, and place it in one tested routine. A mastery check is that you can write a function that accepts parameters, uses default values when appropriate, and returns results reliably for other parts of the program to consume. Second, organizing modules means you separate hardware code, UI code, and web code into named files, and import only what you need. A practical test is building a small project with a sensors module and a display module that import cleanly. Third, using libraries requires familiarity with Python's standard helpers such as json and time and with third-party packages like gpiozero for GPIO control. You should be able to install a package and import it without affecting other projects. Finally, dependency management with virtual environments means you can create, activate, and deactivate an environment, then install packages into it. Misconception: virtual environments are optional — in practice they prevent hard-to-debug conflicts and make deployments repeatable.

A function is a named block of code that performs a single, focused task and can be used repeatedly with different inputs. In Python you declare a function using the def keyword, give it a name, list parameters, and return a value. For example, a function that converts Celsius readings to Fahrenheit encapsulates the formula once so every script reuses the same logic. That reduces duplication and the chance of errors when the formula needs to change. The practical example you will see on the screen shows a conversion routine, an example call that converts twenty five degrees, and a print that outputs the result. A frequent misconception is that functions are only for large programs; in fact, even small scripts benefit because functions make intent explicit and simplify testing. Python supports positional parameters, keyword parameters, and default values that provide sensible fallbacks. The source example describes a sensor with a name, numeric value, and a unit that defaults to the string units when none is supplied. That default helps when a caller doesn't need to specify units every time. Functions may also return multiple values by packaging them into a tuple; consumers can unpack those values as needed. A practical tip is to prefer explicit return values and avoid silently returning None. Before you start coding, remember these three quick reminders: choose descriptive function names and keep each function focused on a single task; split related functions into modules and avoid running hardware code at import time; and use a virtual environment for each project so package versions stay predictable.
